title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
abstract: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.

title: Universal Decoding for Gaussian MIMO-ISI: Spherical Ensembles and Symmetric Neighborhoods
abstract: We construct a universal decoder for cyclic Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with intersymbol interference and unknown channel taps and spatial noise covariance. Codewords are drawn independently and uniformly from a sphere of fixed total energy. Under stated bounds on frequency variation, the decoder attains the ensemble-average error exponent of informed maximum-likelihood decoding for fixed channels and channels with growing memory . We approximate the frequency response by a constant matrix within each frequency block. For this auxiliary channel, every matched log-likelihood is affine in a common sufficient statistic. At fixed received output, we compute the statistic density of an independent competitor. The decoder selects the candidate with the smallest statistic density, equivalently minimizing a weighted sum of residual log-determinants. The density and its support volume give an upper bound on the universal competitor probability. Affinity ensures that at least half of a suitable symmetric neighborhood of the transmitted statistic has matched likelihood no smaller than that of the transmitted word. Integrating a density lower bound over this half gives the matched competitor bound. These bounds establish equality of error exponents, which a Gaussian channel comparison transfers to the original channel. The same decoder attains the matched exponent for independent frequency blocks with prescribed energies satisfying the stated conditions. For energies proportional to block length, an additional gain condition ensures that this exponent is at least that of the total-energy spherical ensemble.

title: GTCRN-SS: Lightweight Causal Speech Separation with Residual Allocation and Reconstruction Refinement
abstract: Low-complexity causal speech separation must preserve speaker information and allocate residual mixture energy without relying on future feature frames. title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
abstract: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.

title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
abstract: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources. We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.

title: TwinHash: Two-Sided Object Identity Management for Time- and Energy-Efficient Agentic Workflows
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) services interleave large language model (LLM) generation with external tool execution, and increasingly rely on search-based workflows that repeatedly revisit shared reasoning states and computations. These patterns create substantial redundancy across tool outputs, LLM responses, and key-value (KV) prefixes, yet existing serving systems primarily optimize shared prompt prefixes, while naive input-keyed caching is unsafe when identical requests produce different outputs. We present TwinHash, a unified object management architecture that assigns each object an input-side hash key to recognize repeated requests and an output-side content fingerprint to validate and locate stored state, complemented by type-specific reuse guards that preserve correctness and response diversity. A software object identity table maintains reusable objects across requests and trajectories, while a hardware object placement table tracks their residency across hierarchical memory tiers so that evicted state can be retrieved rather than recomputed. Across seven agent frameworks and five benchmark suites, reuse follows workflow structure more than benchmark identity. TwinHash serves up to 81% of tool outputs wherever deterministic tool reads recur, and up to 92% of LLM responses in search-based frameworks. Retrieving an evicted KV-prefix from DRAM reduces TTFT by up to 5.6x on Qwen3-32B, with greater gains projected for larger dense models. Under search-based frameworks, TwinHash reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 87% and measured task energy by up to 81% over a prefix-cached baseline, while a per-key serving cap controls the quality-reuse trade-off in adaptive search. These results demonstrate that unified identity, safety, and placement management can convert structural redundancy in emerging agentic workflows into substantial serving-efficiency gains.

title: Attaining Optimal Values under Sure Constraints
abstract: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard specification that must hold on every supported execution, including paths of probability zero. Max uses a pure finite controller; Min may use any pure public-history strategy. We distinguish three numerical questions: can a supplied target be met, can the unspecified optimum be attained, and what is one exact value? For explicit hard and Boolean soft Streett conditions, the strict and non-strict supplied-threshold problems are coNP-complete, attainment of the unsupplied supremum is $\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete, and one exact reduced fraction is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete under polynomial metric reductions. The proofs preserve both the value and its finite attainability when fixing a single opponent, and encode adaptive queries without computing unknown subgame values. The same construction yields matching value-comparison and exact-output lower bounds for ordinary stochastic Streett games with unrestricted randomized history strategies. We also bound the memory needed for optimal finite implementations for arbitrary Muller hard conditions and rational rewards in $[0,1]$ determined by infinitely recurring states. One controller is sure from the entire original sure region and attains at every finitely attained start, with no attainment premise on the other states. For $n$ states in that region it uses $2^{O(n\log(n+1))}Q(1+\log R)$ modes, where $Q$ is the product of the least common denominators of full original chance rows sourced in that sure region and $R$ clears all reward values. Its joint dependence on $Q$ and $R$ is worst-case sharp at each fixed $n\ge6$ when $Q,R\ge2$. Optimal dependence on arena size and efficient general synthesis are not resolved here.

title: The Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis: Detection, Attribution, and Network-Mediated Efficiency
abstract: We propose the Network Adaptive Market Hypothesis (NAMH), a novel extension of the adaptive markets framework that conceptualizes market efficiency as a network-dependent equilibrium emerging from long- memory predictability and cross-market information transmission. Using G20 equity indices and five commodity futures over 2001-2026, we identify Japan as the central information hub, while the United States primarily acts as an information broadcaster. Contrary to conventional expectations, systemic crises do not exhibit higher network spectral radii, challenging the assumption that crisis-related fragility necessarily manifests through increased network amplification. Instead, crisis-related spectral contributions are dominated by Australia and the United States. Importantly, variance-decomposition connectedness is more closely associated with network modularity than with spectral radius, with crisis-period increases driven primarily by cross-cluster spillovers. Notably, efficiency-based market groupings explain network connectedness only marginally compared with geography and asset class, while the middle efficiency tier consistently exhibits the greatest idiosyncratic behaviour.

title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.

title: Low-Rank Iteration for Efficient Calculations of Topological Surface States
abstract: Surface states are hallmarks of topological phases, and their efficient computation is crucial for topology characterization. Conventional supercell methods (SCM) approximate semi-infinite systems as finite periodic ones, but suffer from high computational cost, artificial inter-surface coupling, and slow convergence near band edges. Recently, boundary problems for semi-infinite systems have been recast as block-tridiagonal equations and solved by the cyclic reduction method (CRM) and the transfer matrix method (TMM). However, these approaches remain resource-intensive, as fine-mesh discretization produces very large matrices. Recognizing the intrinsic sparsity and low rank of these matrices, we develop a low-rank iterative method (LIM) with stochastic trace estimation that substantially reduces complexity and memory without sacrificing accuracy, while remaining straightforwardly parallelizable. Benchmarks on 2D and 3D topological systems show orders-of-magnitude acceleration over CRM and TMM. LIM extends readily to heterostructures, defective interfaces, and non-Hermitian systems, providing an efficient platform for topological and plasmonic surface phenomena.

title: From local learning to global electronic properties in large-scale systems
abstract: Machine learning from local atomic environments offers an efficient route to electronic structure, but evaluating global electronic properties in large systems remains computationally demanding. Here we combine real space charge density learning with stochastic propagation using Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians constructed from the predicted densities. The framework avoids target system self-consistent iterations and explicit diagonalization, while hierarchical blocking enables dense grid inference within limited GPU memory . We demonstrate density of states calculations for one million Si atoms and optical and transport calculations for over one hundred thousand atoms, without training separate models for each property. This framework extends the practical scale of electronic structure calculations within Kohn-Sham DFT, opening opportunities to investigate how atomic structure governs electronic, optical and transport properties at length scales relevant to real materials and devices.

title: TouchAnnotator: Multi-Source Tactile Supervision with Privileged-View Distillation
abstract: Egocentric video captures human-object interaction at scale but rarely includes tactile labels for hidden contact and pressure. We introduce TouchAnnotator, an ego-only bimanual tactile annotator trained with multi-source tactile supervision and privileged-view distillation. A canonical hand field unifies glove pressure, geometry-derived human contact, and robot fingertip deformation from six datasets and three embodiments, while source-aware masks preserve valid targets. During training, an EMA teacher observes synchronized ego and wrist views and distills hand-local representations and tactile predictions into a student that uses only ego video and estimated pose at inference. Compact past-clip memory supplies temporal context. We evaluate on EgoTouch, zero-shot FPHA transfer, and 860 synchronized glove recordings. The model transfers to bare-hand contact and produces qualitatively coherent tactile responses across bare-hand, gloved-hand, and robot embodiments. On measured recordings, it improves temporal accuracy by 5.38 points and Volumetric IoU by 5.02 points under a shared protocol. These results show that heterogeneous human--robot supervision and privileged training views can turn egocentric video into dense tactile annotations.

title: PhoPunct: A Large-Scale Benchmark of Transformer Architectures for Vietnamese Punctuation Restoration
abstract: Vietnamese punctuation restoration is often evaluated on relatively small benchmarks, limiting conclusions about how architectural choices scale with data volume. We present a controlled benchmark on News and Novels corpora containing 22.1 million labeled tokens (19.9M News and 2.2M Novels). We evaluate 17 architectures formed from four pretrained Transformer backbones and optional bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) and conditional random field (CRF) layers, together with a PhoBERT-large-Bi-LSTM-CRF model, PhoPunct. Every model is trained for eight epochs with the same learning rate and without architecture-specific tuning. Under this fixed budget, adding Bi-LSTM and CRF layers does not reliably improve macro F1: in seven of eight matched domain-backbone comparisons, a plain Transformer classifier matches or outperforms its Bi-LSTM-CRF counterpart. PhoPunct obtains the best News result (61.35), whereas XLM-R with a CRF obtains the best Novels result (50.18), exceeding PhoPunct (48.97). These results show that the value of recurrent and structured-prediction heads depends on their optimization regime and motivate explicit separation between architectural improvements and improvements due to architecture-specific tuning. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/aisia-research-lab/PhoPunct

title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.

title: EventHOI: Event-Driven Resource-Efficient Hand-Object Interaction Logging on Smartglasses
abstract: Hand-object interactions (HOIs) can be captured by smartglasses to learn how people manipulate objects in daily life. Automatic logging of these interactions from an egocentric perspective provides time-stamped evidence of daily actions for applications like memory assistance. However, continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses. We present EventHOI, an event-driven sensing and compression system that couples selective RGB capture with HOI-aware encoding to enable egocentric logging over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) while preserving downstream HOI logging performance. title: Training-Free Active Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.

title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.

title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.

title: Landauer bound in a regular Bardeen black hole: extremality and evaporation
abstract: Does the vanishing Hawking temperature of an extremal black hole imply that information can be erased without energy transfer? We investigate this question in the regular Bardeen geometry using a two-level quantum system, representing a quantum memory , coupled to a scalar bosonic field confined within an exterior cavity. The Hawking temperature tends to zero at extremality, as does the corresponding thermal Landauer scale. The field in an exterior cavity behaves differently, provided both walls remain away from the horizon, its lowest excitation energy stays finite. For a maximally mixed memory coupled to a reservoir initially in its unique ground state, we find $Q_\infty\geqΔ_{R,\infty}(1/2-ε)$, with $Δ_{R,\infty}$ the reservoir gap and $ε$ the reset error. For a resonant single-mode interaction, we give a reset protocol that attains the bound with no work supplied by the external control. In this example, the memory itself supplies the energy gained by the field. In the multimode calculation, counter-rotating terms are retained. Keeping the pulse parameters unchanged, we find a larger residual reset error closer to extremality. For reservoirs prepared thermally, we evaluate the Reeb--Wolf balance and find that the relative-entropy contribution, expressed in energy units, can have a finite low-temperature limit. These numerical preparations are externally imposed and remain hotter than the Hawking temperature. For comparison, an unconfined scalar field has near-extremal luminosity $P_\infty\propto y^4$, with $y=r_H/|g|-\sqrt2$. Assuming a particular quasistatic energy-loss prescription gives $y\propto t^{-1/2}$; this does not establish the existence of a stable remnant. For this particular reset operation, vanishing Hawking temperature therefore does not force the transferred heat to vanish.

title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

title: MESAM: Enhancing SAM2 for Few-Shot Segmentation through Semantic-Visual Memory Generation and Refinement
abstract: This paper investigates how to leverage the powerful capabilities of the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) to tackle few-shot segmentation (FSS) tasks. One major challenge lies in the substantial appearance differences between the support and query images, which may diminish the effectiveness of the memory -matching process in SAM2. Through systematic analysis, we find that the memory generated based on the categorical semantic information is robust to this appearance divergence and is more compatible with SAM2. Based on these observations, we propose a new Memory -Enhanced SAM2 (MESAM) method, which first introduces a Semantic-Visual Memory Generation (SVMG) module to separately construct a query semantic memory , a query foreground visual memory , and a support adaptive visual memory . Then, in our designed Interactive Semantic Memory Refinement (ISMR) module, we further enrich the obtained semantic memory with fine-grained visual details, and suppress its misatcivated background responses. Extensive experiments on the PASCAL-$5^i$, COCO-$20^i$, and LVIS-$92^i$ datasets demonstrate that MESAM consistently outperforms existing FSS methods, achieving new state-of-the-art segmentation performance. title: ODD+LLM: Specifying LLM-Agent Behavior for Reproducible Social Simulation
abstract: The ODD protocol is the de facto standard for describing agent-based models, but it lacks vocabulary for the components that determine LLM-agent behavior: prompt assembly, memory serialization, parsing, and retry logic. We propose ODD+LLM, a backward-compatible extension adding five documentation blocks grounded in the CoALA cognitive-architecture framework. To show that the gap matters, we conduct a multiverse analysis [Steegen et al., 2016] of a published LLM naming-game simulation, varying six specification choices a reimplementer must make. Variants that are defensible readings of the paper stay within statistical noise of our baseline reconstruction. Missing one instruction that the paper states but is easy to overlook (that the model answers as an outside observer rather than as a player) raises the share of runs settling on the convention agents individually favor from 0.35 to 1.00 and makes convergence three times faster, in a reimplementation that uses a different model from the original. We complement the demonstration with a reconstruction-sufficiency review of 28 published LLM-agent simulations, finding that the details of how prompts are built and how model outputs are parsed are undetermined in 77% of cases, and that no paper fully specifies its main LLM call. ODD+LLM gives the field a standard home for information it already produces but currently scatters across code repositories, supplementary files, and undocumented defaults.

title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory -Efficient Quantization Aware Training
abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory -efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

title: Snow Changes Drought Characterization but Not Drought Predictability: A Leakage-Free Multiscale Study in Ohio
abstract: We examine whether accounting for snow accumulation and melt, which precipitation-based drought indices ignore, changes drought characterization and one-month-ahead drought forecasting at three stations in Ohio, USA (1953--2026). The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is compared with the Standardized Snow Melt and Rain Index (SMRI), and both are decomposed with the Haar maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform. Nonlinear autoregressive networks without (NAR) and with (NARX) wavelet inputs are compared over 100 paired repetitions in a leakage-free design (past-only wavelet inputs, untouched test period), together with persistence, climatology, and linear autoregressive benchmarks. Snow changes the 3-month index mainly from December to May (mean absolute SMRI--SPI differences of up to 0.17--0.28). These differences are attributable to the snow-adjusted input rather than to the fitted distribution, are robust to the snow-model parameters, and change the drought classification of 21--32\% of the December--May drought months. Wavelet inputs reduce NARX error relative to NAR by 6--10\% for the 3-month indices in 92--100\% of the repetitions, but not for the 6-month indices. A linear autoregression with 7--12 lags is at least as accurate as two-lag NARX for every series, and networks given six lags gain at most 4.5\% from the wavelet inputs and only match the autoregression. The forecast gain therefore reflects the memory of the accumulated index rather than multiscale information, and it is similar for the SPI and the SMRI. Snow matters for drought monitoring in winter and spring, but not for one-month predictability.

title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.

title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

title: Stochastic AI Model Placement for AI-and-RAN Coexistence in 6G Networks
abstract: This paper considers AI-service placement over geographically distributed RAN sites equipped with GPU resources partitioned into fixed, isolated multi-instance GPU (MIG) profiles. We propose C$^2$AIR, a chance-constrained optimization model that maximizes expected AI requests served while protecting uncertain RAN workloads and enforcing probabilistic capacity reliability requirements for admitted AI services. C$^2$AIR allows a service to run at multiple sites and accounts for discrete profile, memory , and GPU-slice constraints. We evaluate C$^2$AIR on a four-site deployment calibrated from NVIDIA Aerial RAN capacity figures and MLPerf Inference results, and on seven larger scenarios with up to 15 sites and 40 AI services, computing every violation and overload probability exactly from the demand distributions. C$^2$AIR keeps the RAN violation probability within its target at every hour of the day, whereas reserving for the mean RAN demand violates it in 24\% to 47\% of the intervals. The reliability condition prevents placing AI models that would be overloaded in 85\% of the intervals at an event hour, and multi-site replication serves 2.7 times more AI requests than single-site deployment. The evaluation also shows that coarse MIG instances and a heavy demand tail can make strict RAN protection expensive.

title: SEU Hardened Multi-Context Spintronic FPGA
abstract: Due to susceptibility to radiation-induced soft errors and resource constraints implementing large and complex designs on field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) in harsh environments is challenging. Therefore, to mitigate these issues, this paper proposes an innovative approach through the introduction of a single event upset (SEU)-hardened spintronic FPGA architecture that incorporates multi-context capabilities. Leveraging the non-volatile properties of magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ), the proposed design can store two/four distinct configurations internally, eliminating the dependence on external non-volatile memory which significantly boosts the system performance. Additionally, through post-layout simulation, we demonstrate our design immunity to SEU, which enhances its reliability and operational stability in environments susceptible to radiation-induced soft errors. The efficiency of the proposed design was also evaluated using the ROSSETA benchmark, which serves as a representative model for real-world FPGA applications.

title: Analytical mean-field model for electrochemical metallization memristors with a nanoporous matrix: application to Ag/anodic alumina/Al
abstract: Memristors based on electrochemical metallization with many filaments are usually modeled by microscopic simulations with many parameters or by phenomenological laws whose parameters are hard to relate to physical quantities. We present an analytical mean-field model for a population of Ag filaments confined in the pores of a nanoporous matrix, built on Ohm's law, Faraday's law and a power-based rupture criterion. The filaments have a truncated normal distribution of cross-sections and rupture leaving lognormally distributed gaps whose median grows with the dissipated power. Gap closing shifts the distribution of squared gaps rigidly, and the model therefore admits closed-form expressions for the switching voltage, the read current, the rupture branch and the high-voltage current. We apply it to Ag/nanoporous anodic alumina/Al structures fabricated from industrial-grade aluminum, with a 2.4$μ$m alumina layer, and measured under ambient conditions. The parameters were fitted to the bipolar sweeps, with the gap dispersion taken from the temporal shape of the read after a pulse. They reproduce the bipolar response, including voltage-controlled negative differential resistance, and predict without refitting the unipolar sweeps and the amplitude of the pulse response, where state memory appears. A second sample, with a larger contact deposited chemically, is described by the same model. In vacuum the devices neither switch nor show negative differential resistance, as expected if adsorbed water supplies the counter reaction; the residual high-voltage current follows ionic hopping conduction.

title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support
abstract: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.

title: The GPU Needs an Operating System
abstract: AI chips sit mostly idle while serving models, because replies must be fast and each step waits on memory . On two large open models, the math units were busy only about 6-11% of the time. We argue the GPU needs an operating system that keeps urgent work on schedule and fills idle capacity with other useful work. A feature that ships today recovers a quarter of a GPU with work designed to share, and a tenth with real jobs, at 5% slower decode. Our research system does better: one resident kernel runs a whole model faster than vLLM's best for a single request, and shares the GPU at under 2% slowdown. Scaling beyond one hand-built model needs compilers and a few new chip features, which we specify.

title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.

title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
abstract: Analog compute-in- memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

title: Dynamic GPU Voxel Grids and Voxel-sequential Processing in NanoVDB
abstract: We introduce two fundamental advances to the NanoVDB data structure: dynamic GPU-native topological updates, and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that dramatically accelerates point-wise and stencil-based operators on sparse grids. NanoVDB's linearized memory layout has delivered strong GPU performance, and the Index-Grid concept introduced in the fVDB framework [Williams et al 2024] provided topology/data separation and optimal compactness of storage in sparse machine learning workloads. However, all these prior iterations of NanoVDB assume a static topology that has precluded use of this data structure in simulation and dynamic geometric processes. We eliminate this limitation by introducing a suite of dynamic topology operators -- morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement. These operators use bit-parallel algorithms to reconstruct grids containing hundreds of millions of voxels in just a few milliseconds. We also introduce a voxel-sequential access paradigm and data structure for GPU kernels operating on sparse data. We stream active voxels as a flat linear sequence, minimizing or eliminating the need for tree traversal in the process. This achieves compute density and regularity that allow even complex stencil-based operators to approach peak memory bandwidth, with minimal storage overhead. Together, these contributions remove the read-only constraint from NanoVDB, establishing it as a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation. We evaluate the efficacy of our newly introduced operators in benchmarks sourced from applications such as 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation, and large-scale mesh voxelization.

title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.

title: Modulation Induced Memory Resonances in Dynamically Driven Optical Cavities
abstract: Temporal modulation of optical cavities provides a powerful mechanism for controlling photonic states beyond the static cavity paradigm. Here, we investigate the dynamics of periodically driven optical cavities using a time-dependent cavity-field model with modulated resonance frequencies. We demonstrate modulation-induced tuning of cavity resonances and analyze the resulting intracavity field evolution in both amplitude and phase. The interplay between periodic modulation and cavity dissipation gives rise to pronounced hysteretic behavior, revealing memory effects associated with the finite photon lifetime of the cavity. By quantifying the hysteresis area as a function of modulation frequency, we identify distinct memory resonances characterized by enhanced field-history dependence at specific driving frequencies. Furthermore, we examine the time-resolved local density of optical states (LDOS) and show that temporal modulation enables dynamic spectral redistribution of photonic states, with the degree of confinement governed by the cavity loss rate. Our results establish a simple framework for understanding and engineering memory effects in dynamically driven optical resonators and provide new opportunities for tunable photonic environments, dynamic LDOS control, and reconfigurable light-matter interactions.

title: Density kernel and temporal quantum information probes in double-scaled SYK
abstract: Entanglement is conventionally defined through a Hilbert space bipartition on a fixed time slice. Recent work has generalized this notion to multiple times through a non-Hermitian density kernel constructed from temporal correlation functions, encoding causal response, temporal non-classicality and quantum dynamics. We construct this kernel in the double-scaled Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (DSSYK) model using its exact chord Hilbert space formulation and study the resulting temporal information diagnostics. The direct sum structure of chord space naturally introduces a coarse-graining under which coherence between different chord sectors is removed. We show that the corresponding kernel measures quantify how information is dynamically transferred across subregions in the chord Hilbert space. We find that decreasing $λ$ enhances the propagation of temporal correlation across chord sectors, as well as the loss of memory within a fixed sector. This accelerated temporal dynamics in the small $λ$ limit coincides with the emergence of a semiclassical gravity description. Depending on the chord space partition, the probes exhibit either saturation, a growth followed by a decay, or temporary memory loss. The characteristic propagation time is nicely captured by a wavefront picture in Krylov space, with position-dependent hopping parameters that are determined by the DSSYK Lanczos coefficients. Finally, given the quantum sine-dilaton gravity description of DSSYK and its connections to de Sitter holography, our results provide a controlled setting for probing temporal quantum correlations across quantum and semiclassical gravitational regimes, and motivate a geometric interpretation of the density kernel.

title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, naïve per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory , loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

title: MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
abstract: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. title: Synaptic Multi-Weight Wafer-Scale Domain Wall Magnetic Tunnel Junctions Driven by Spin Orbit Torque
abstract: Spintronic synaptic devices based on magnetic random access memory (MRAM) are a rapidly evolving class within the analog neuromorphic architecture. However, obtaining the multi-weight or analog behavior desired for improved neural network inference accuracy in scaled MRAM remains a challenge. In this study, we demonstrate and tune up to eight distinct resistance levels in 300 mm wafer-scale magnetic tunnel junction artificial synapses driven by spin orbit torque. By varying the applied in-plane field, multi-weight resistance states emerge through domain wall nucleation and pinning. These multi-weight states appear stochastically and can be addressed with an iterative programming algorithm to program a specific resistance. Electromagnetic simulations indicate the multiple states are due to domain wall nucleation mediated by in-plane field and applied voltage. Implementation of the measured multi-weight devices in a neural network yields a 96.1% inference accuracy using the MNIST dataset if all devices provide the same number of multi-weight states. When experimental device-to-device variation is included, the accuracy is 48.6%. Overall, this work demonstrates a route towards multi-weight artificial synapse MRAM, establishing a path towards scalable neuromorphic systems based on spintronics.

title: Scaling Up Analog CIM: A Simulation Framework for Topology-Aware Mapping
abstract: Analog compute-in- memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient AI inference by performing in-situ matrix multiplication. The growing demand for deploying larger models motivates chiplet integration to expand CIM capacity. However, simulation abstractions based on local operator costs and aggregate communication metrics obscure the impact of weight-mapping topology when CIM system scales up. We develop a phase analysis that quantifies how strongly mapping topology affects system performance across hardware configurations and how mapping optimization translates into latency gains. To evaluate and exploit this design space, we present Isobar, a simulation platform integrating CIM decompositions, heterogeneous execution, and resource modeling. Validated against silicon measurements and cycle-accurate simulation, Isobar provides reliable cost estimates that enable effective mapping search across model and hardware configurations. For Gemma-7B prefill, Isobar-guided mapping reduces communication time by 23.3% and end-to-end latency by 18.6% relative to the strongest baseline. Isobar's system-level modeling show that analog CIM retains energy-efficiency potential relative to GPU when scaled to thousands of dies, and identify topology-aware mapping as a key design dimension for efficient execution.

title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
abstract: Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories , however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
abstract: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory , and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory . After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

title: StrataFlux: Memory -Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified- memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory . These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

title: Connectivity in a New Bounded-Space Dynamic Model
abstract: We introduce a new model for dynamic algorithms in which the algorithm has read-only oracle access to a dynamically changing input and random access to its own bounded workspace. It is a dynamic analogue of the time-space tradeoffs for static inputs studied in complexity theory, where only writable memory counts as space. We study dynamic undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity: after every edge update to an $n$-vertex graph, an algorithm with $S$ words of workspace must report whether $s$ and $t$ are connected. The graph is accessed via adjacency list queries (degree, $j$-th neighbor) or adjacency matrix queries. Our algorithms are randomized; our lower bounds hold for randomized algorithms with $cn$ bits of workspace, $c>0$ a small constant ($cn/\log n$ for the worst-case matrix bound). We prove: (1) With adjacency lists, worst-case time $\tildeΘ(n^2/S^2)$ per insertion is necessary and sufficient for incremental algorithms. (2) With an adjacency matrix, worst-case time $\tildeΩ(n^2/S)$ per insertion is necessary for incremental algorithms, and sufficient for $S\ge\sqrt{n}$. (3) With amortization, incremental algorithms achieve $\tilde O(n/S)$ time per insertion with adjacency lists and $\tilde O(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, while $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n/S})$ and $\tildeΩ(n\sqrt{n/S})$, respectively, are necessary. (4) Fully dynamic algorithms need amortized time $\tildeΩ(n/S)$ per update with adjacency lists and $\tildeΩ(n^2/S)$ with an adjacency matrix, even on forests, where both bounds are tight (lists: under bounded degree). Conventional dynamic connectivity admits polylogarithmic update time with $Ω(n)$ words of space. In contrast, our lower bounds show that polynomial update time is necessary whenever $S\le n^{1-\varepsilon}$, even for a single pair of vertices and even for incremental algorithms with amortized guarantees.

title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory
abstract: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-\nu_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
